title: Atlas and Typewriter
premise: In the port city of Vellamare, on the eve of revolution, Coral Lockridge works her late father's typeface bench in a print shop that has seen better decades. When Emeric Voss arrives carrying letters in handwriting identical to that of executed pamphleteer Aldous Ren — officially dead for two years — the two are drawn into a conspiracy to prove the rebellion's martyr lives, or lived long enough to be betrayed by the men now claiming his legacy. Racing the victors' historians and a general amnesty that will burn the archives, they must set the truth in type and smuggle it aboard the morning ship. The book ends with the printed record sailing free as Voss is taken, leaving Coral to inherit not just the shop but the burden of what survives in ink.
about_author: Isandro Vasquez is a former letterpress compositor who spent a decade restoring antique printing equipment in coastal trading towns before turning to fiction. He writes historical novels about the people who handle other people's words.

chapters.title: The Weight of Lead
chapters.summary: Coral Lockridge's POV. In the failing print shop of Vellamare, Coral cuts typefaces by lamplight while revolution gathers beyond the harbor like weather she refuses to acknowledge. Her father's death left her the shop and its debts. Emotional beat: quiet denial — history is something that happens to other people.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Composing Stick
chapters.summary: Emeric Voss arrives soaked from the packet boat, asking for a printer who can verify handwriting. He carries letters signed by Aldous Ren, the executed pamphleteer whose martyrdom lit the revolution's fuse. Coral recognizes the hand instantly — she cut the original matrices herself. Beat: the impossible made physical.

chapters.title: Ink Remembers
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Comparing the letters against her father's archived proofs, she confirms the writing is genuine — yet dated months after Ren's public execution. Fear replaces skepticism; someone forged a corpse, or faked one. Beat: the shop stops being a refuge and becomes evidence.

chapters.title: What the Martyr Cost
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Flashback to his years as Ren's courier: the real man was exhausted, compromised, and planning to expose his own committee before he vanished. Voss believes Ren escaped alive. Beat: hero worship curdling into harder knowledge about the man behind the myth.

chapters.title: The Committee of the Dawn
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Revolutionary leader Cassian Mereau visits the shop, charming and watchful, commissioning victory broadsides. He asks too precisely whether any of Ren's papers have surfaced. Beat: power arriving with a smile, and Coral learning to lie with a straight face.

chapters.title: Bargains in Bitter Type
chapters.summary: Voss and Coral form an uneasy alliance: she has the craft, he has the contacts. They discover the letters implicate Mereau in selling Ren out to the old regime before the uprising. Beat: reluctant trust, sealed over a shared pot of coffee and mutual suspicion.

chapters.title: The Archive Burns Early
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. The provisional government begins 'reorganizing' records; a neighboring print house is torched with its archive inside. Coral hides her father's proof books beneath the floor of the type cellar. Beat: grief weaponized into resolve.

chapters.title: A Hand in the Crowd
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Following a rumor, Voss glimpses a man with Ren's distinctive gait in the fish market — then loses him as soldiers sweep the quarter. He returns beaten and doubting. Beat: hope as a thing that gets you hurt.

chapters.title: The Apprentice Who Watched
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Young apprentice Tibo reveals he once delivered a parcel for her father to a lighthouse keeper on Gray Skerry — after Ren's supposed death. The shop held secrets Coral never suspected. Beat: inheritance redefined as obligation, not property.

chapters.title: Gray Skerry
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. A dangerous crossing to the skerry yields a hidden cache: Ren's final testament naming his betrayers, plus proof he died of fever weeks after escaping — a martyr twice over, and unable to speak for himself now. Beat: the truth is smaller and sadder than the legend.

chapters.title: Setting the Truth
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Back in the cellar, Coral and Voss begin setting Ren's testament by night, one page at a time, using discarded matrices so no record exists but the metal itself. Beat: intimacy forged through shared labor and ticking time.

chapters.title: Mereau's Generosity
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Mereau offers Voss an official post as the revolution's chronicler — and subtly threatens Coral's shop. Accepting means access; accepting means complicity. Beat: temptation dressed as honor, the first taste of corruption's price.

chapters.title: The Informant in the Loft
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Tibo is caught copying a page of the testament; he confesses Mereau's men have been watching the shop for weeks. Coral must decide whether the boy betrayed them or saved them. Beat: betrayal and mercy tangled together.

chapters.title: Amnesty and Ash
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. The government announces a general amnesty paired with an official history — all private papers deemed seditious will be destroyed within days. The morning tide ship becomes the only way the testament leaves the country. Beat: the clock starts audibly ticking.

chapters.title: What We Owe the Dead
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Coral argues for staying and defending the shop; Voss argues the record matters more than any building. Their fight exposes the book's core question — what survival costs, and who pays it. Beat: the alliance cracks under pressure.

chapters.title: The Printer's Daughter Decides
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Finding her father's hidden ledger — payments he took from Ren himself — Coral understands he chose survival over truth once, and it hollowed him. She chooses differently. Beat: breaking the inherited pattern; resolve hardens into steel.

chapters.title: Night Press Run
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. They print forty copies of the testament through the night as soldiers patrol outside. Tibo keeps watch; Mereau's men close in at dawn. Beat: breathless momentum, the press clattering like a heartbeat.

chapters.title: The Harbor at First Light
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Smuggling the copies through checkpoints in paper bales, Coral reaches the quay as Mereau confronts Voss publicly, offering pardon for silence. Voss refuses on the record, loudly, before witnesses. Beat: courage as performance that makes retreat impossible.

chapters.title: Taken
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Soldiers seize Voss; the bales go aboard without him. From the dock he sees the ship weigh anchor carrying the truth he cannot follow. Beat: sacrifice completed — the price of survival paid by the one who doesn't survive intact.

chapters.title: The Victor's Historian
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Mereau visits the shop one last time, offering to spare it if Coral prints his official version. She agrees aloud — and shows him the empty type cellar, the matrices already melted. Beat: a duel of smiles; power meets quiet defiance.

chapters.title: Copies Abroad
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Weeks later, word returns: the testament has surfaced in foreign papers, forcing even Mereau's allies to distance themselves. Ren's true story spreads faster than any correction can chase it. Beat: vindication at a distance, bittersweet and incomplete.

chapters.title: The Open Case
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Coral reopens the shop, trains Tibo, and sets new type — including a single line honoring Voss, still imprisoned. History happened to her after all; now she makes it. Beat: inheritance fulfilled — the price paid, the record kept, the work continuing.
